claim: 81.5% (2515 molecules) of human membrane proteins in the UniProt database have been reported or predicted to be glycosylated.
source: We first selected all human membrane proteins in the database (UniProt) based on the presence of a transmembrane domain or membrane anchor domain and found that 81.5% (2515 molecules) of these membrane proteins had previously been reported or predicted to be glycosylated (Bateman et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the UniProt database analysis and is cited with a reference (Bateman et al., 2023).

claim: Both NetNGlyc/NetOGlyc and GlycoEP software packages predicted O- or N-glycosylation in 2441 and 2290 proteins respectively, with 2226 molecules (88.5% of the total) predicted by both software packages.
source: Both software packages predicted one or more O- or N-glycosylation in 2441 and 2290 proteins, respectively, of which 2226 molecules (88.5% of the total) were predicted by both software packages (Figure 1B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational predictions from two software packages and is illustrated in figures.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient between the predicted glycosylation rates of all molecules calculated by each software was 0.656.
source: The Pearson correlation coefficient between the predicted glycosylation rates of all molecules calculated by each software was 0.656 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the software predictions.

claim: Both software programs detected three times as many sequences predicted to undergo O-type glycosylation as those predicted to undergo N-type glycosylation.
source: Both software programs also detected three times as many sequences predicted to undergo O-type glycosylation as those predicted to undergo N-type glycosylation (3.08 and 3.00 times more, respectively), and this trend was particularly pronounced for highly glycosylated molecules.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational predictions from the software analysis.

claim: The measured PNA/mol for sample molecules correlated linearly with the predicted number of glycosylation sites.
source: We evaluated the correlation between the experimentally determined PNA/mol and the predicted number of glycosylation sites for each protein and found that the two were indeed in a linear relationship (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of lectin binding correlated with computational predictions.

claim: All highly glycosylated proteins, with the exception of GYPC, had an inhibitory effect on SARS-CoV2-PP infection.
source: The results showed that all highly glycosylated proteins, with the exception of GYPC, which has the shortest ectodomain, had an inhibitory effect on infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental infection assay data.

claim: The range of mean densities at which highly glycosylated molecules could inhibit infection was approximately 100 μm–2, which is an order of magnitude lower than the density required for membrane-bound synthetic PEGs (2000 μm–2).
source: Previous results showed that membrane-bound synthetic polyethyleneglycols (PEGs) inhibit SARS-CoV-2-PP infection at surface density above 2000 μm–2 (Kaizuka and Machida, 2023). In contrast, the range of mean densities at which highly glycosylated molecules could inhibit infection was an order of magnitude lower, ~100 μm–2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and comparison with previously published results (Kaizuka and Machida, 2023).

claim: IC50 was inversely correlated with the amount of glycosylation of each molecule (Pearson correlation coefficient, –0.29).
source: We found that IC50 was inversely correlated with the amount of glycosylation of each molecule (Pearson correlation coefficient, –0.29; Figure 1G)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental infection inhibition data.

claim: IC50 was correlated with molecular weight including glycans (correlation coefficient of –0.39) but not significantly correlated with amino acid length (correlation coefficient of 0.11).
source: IC50 was similarly correlated with the molecular weight including glycans, but was not significantly correlated with amino acid length (correlation coefficient of –0.39 and 0.11, respectively; Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A typical glycoprotein in the experimental system is glycosylated at approximately 50% of the predicted sites, assuming the average size of O-glycans as decasaccharides with a molecular weight of approximately 2000.
source: From these data, we can estimate that a typical glycoprotein in our system is glycosylated at ~50% of the predicted sites by assuming the average size of O-glycans as decasaccharides with a molecular weight of ~2000.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data on glycan mass in purified proteins.

claim: Highly infected cells were spatially exclusive with highly glycan-expressing cells in Calu-3 epithelial cell monolayers.
source: We found that highly infected cells were spatially exclusive with highly glycan-expressing cells, indicating that there was a clear inverse correlation between the amount of virus infection and the amount of surface-bound lectins in the cells (Figure 2AB).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy imaging data showing spatial distribution patterns.

claim: The inverse correlation between infection and glycans was most pronounced when quantifying N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5AC) compared to various types of glycans.
source: In this cell line, this inverse correlation was most pronounced when quantifying N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5AC, recognized by lectins SSA and MAL) compared to the various types of glycans, while some other glycans also showed weak correlations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements using different lectins specific for different glycan types.

claim: CD44, which accounts for about 10% of all cell surface glycans, showed a weak inverse correlation with viral infection.
source: CD44, which was shown to account for about 10% of all cell surface glycans (Wyler et al., 2021), showed a weak inverse correlation with viral infection
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and cited with a reference (Wyler et al., 2021).

claim: ERBB2 is approximately four-fold more highly expressed than CD44.
source: even such a weak correlation was not observed with other proteins, including ERBB2, which is approximately four-fold more highly expressed than CD44 (Figure 2C-D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in figures.

claim: The amount of glycans on cells did not correlate with the expression of CD44 alone or any other specific protein.
source: Furthermore, the amount of glycans on the cells did not correlate with the expression of CD44 alone or any other specific protein, suggesting that all the different glycoproteins contributed to the total glycan content in an additive manner (Figure 2E-F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of glycan content and protein expression.

claim: A large number of SARS-CoV2-PP can bind to cells even when cells expressed sufficient amounts of glycoprotein (mean density ~50 µm–2) that could inhibit viral infection.
source: We found that a large number of SARS-CoV2-PP can still bind to cells even when cells expressed sufficient amounts of the glycoprotein (mean density ~50 µm–2) that could account for the majority of glycans within these cells and inhibit viral infection (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental virus binding assay data.

claim: On the two-dimensional culture surface of Calu-3 cells, no negative correlation was observed between the number of viruses bound and the total amount of glycans on the cell surface.
source: Similarly, on the two-dimensional culture surface of Calu-3 cells, no negative correlation was observed between the number of viruses bound and the total amount of glycans on the cell surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of virus binding and glycan content.

claim: Glycoproteins do not inhibit virus binding to cells, but rather inhibit the steps required for subsequent virus internalization.
source: These results indicate that glycoproteins do not inhibit virus binding to cells, but rather inhibit the steps required for subsequent virus internalization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental virus binding and infection data.

claim: Expression of MUC1 with higher number of tandem repeats reduced the dextran transport in the fluid phase.
source: Expression of MUC1 with higher number of tandem repeats reduced the dextran transport in the fluid phase, while expression of multiple membrane glycoproteins that have infection inhibitory effects, including truncated MUC1 molecules, showed no effect on fluid phase endocytosis, indicating a molecular weight-dependent effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental endocytosis assay data.

claim: The measured Flory radius (RF) from FLIM-FRET was strongly correlated with the molecular weight including glycans (correlation coefficient of 0.87) but weakly correlated with the number of amino acids (correlation coefficient of 0.58).
source: We found that RF was strongly correlated with the molecular weight including glycans, but weakly correlated with the number of amino acids (correlation coefficient of 0.87 and 0.58, respectively; Figure 4D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of FLIM-FRET measurements.

claim: The scaling exponent ν in the Flory model for highly glycosylated molecules (MUC1, CD43, CD164, CD24) was 0.144, while for low glycosylated molecules it was 0.108.
source: We estimated ν separately for highly glycosylated molecules (MUC1, CD43, CD164, CD24) and for low glycosylated molecules. The resulting ν for the two groups are 0.144 and 0.108, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of FLIM-FRET data using the Flory model.

claim: The upper limit of the Flory radius of the extracellular domains of all membrane proteins in the human genome is approximately 10.5 nm.
source: This calculation also gives a rough estimate of the upper limit of the RF of the extracellular domains of all membrane proteins in the human genome (approximately 10.5 nm).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation using the Flory model with estimated scaling exponents.

claim: Non-glycosylated recombinant CD43 and MUC1(14TR) ectodomain produced in E. coli bound at an estimated average saturation density of more than 10,000 molecules μm–2.
source: The non-glycosylated recombinant CD43 and MUC1(14TR) ectodomain produced in E. coli bound at an estimated average saturation density of more than 10,000 molecules μm–2, while the glycosylated CD43 and MUC1 ectodomain produced in HEK 293T cells bound at much lower saturation densities (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of protein binding to lipid bilayers.

claim: Glycosylated CD43 and MUC1 ectodomain produced in HEK 293T cells bound at much lower saturation densities than non-glycosylated versions.
source: The non-glycosylated recombinant CD43 and MUC1(14TR) ectodomain produced in E. coli bound at an estimated average saturation density of more than 10,000 molecules μm–2, while the glycosylated CD43 and MUC1 ectodomain produced in HEK 293T cells bound at much lower saturation densities (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of protein binding to lipid bilayers.

claim: Dissociation constants for membrane-bound glycosylated proteins (0.61 μM and 0.48 μM for CD43 and MUC1, respectively) were similar to or lower than those for bacterial proteins (3.84 μM and 12.6 μM for CD43 and MUC1, respectively).
source: Dissociation constants for membrane-bound glycosylated (g-) proteins (0.61 μM and 0.48 μM for CD43 and MUC1, respectively) were similar to or lower than those for bacterial (b-) proteins (3.84 μM and 12.6 μM for CD43 and MUC1, respectively), indicating that differences in molecular affinity for the lipid bilayer are not responsible for the large differences in saturation binding densities.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of protein binding kinetics.

claim: Both glycosylated and non-glycosylated proteins were equally diffusible as individual molecules on lipid bilayers.
source: single molecule tracking experiments confirmed that both glycosylated (g-) and non-glycosylated and bacterial (b-) proteins were equally diffusible as individual molecules (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by single molecule tracking experimental data.

claim: The coverage of highly glycosylated proteins at binding saturation was approximately 20% for g-MUC1 and approximately 40% for g-CD43.
source: Under this assumption, the coverage of highly glycosylated proteins at binding saturation was ~20% for g-MUC1 and ~40% for g-CD43, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from experimental binding data assuming hemispherical protein geometry.

claim: The coverage of b-CD43 and b-MUC1 at saturated binding was estimated to be greater than 100% under the normalization standard of hemispherical RF.
source: In contrast, the coverage of b-CD43 and b-MUC1 at saturated binding was estimated to be greater than 100% under this normalization standard, indicating that the mean projected sizes of these molecules in surface direction were smaller than those expected from their RF.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from experimental binding data assuming hemispherical protein geometry.

claim: Glycosylation reduces the saturation density of membrane proteins, regardless of molecular size.
source: Thus, it is clear that glycosylation reduces the saturation density of membrane proteins, regardless of molecular size.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental protein binding data comparing glycosylated and non-glycosylated proteins.

claim: No significant changes in protein binding between fluid and nonfluid bilayers were observed for both b-MUC1 and g-MUC1 molecules.
source: No significant changes in protein binding between fluid and nonfluid bilayers were observed for both b-MUC1 and g-MUC1 molecules (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements comparing protein binding to different types of lipid bilayers.

claim: Membrane fluidity does not affect the average intermolecular distance or other relevant parameters that control molecular binding in the reconstituted system.
source: This result suggests that membrane fluidity does not affect the average intermolecular distance or other relevant parameters that control molecular binding in the reconstituted system.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing protein binding to fluid and nonfluid bilayers.

claim: Membrane proteins above a certain threshold size are excluded from the virus-cell interface, regardless of the degree of glycosylation.
source: These results showed that membrane proteins above a certain threshold size are excluded from the virus-cell interface, regardless of the degree of glycosylation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from STORM imaging data showing protein distribution at virus-cell interfaces.

claim: The transition from low-exclusion regime to high-exclusion regime occurred nonlinearly and abruptly with protein size.
source: Interestingly, the transition from low-exclusion regime to high-exclusion regime occurred nonlinearly and abruptly with protein size (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of STORM imaging data showing protein exclusion patterns.

claim: The overall correlation between Flory radius and density_(in/out) was calculated to be –0.36.
source: Nevertheless, the overall correlation between Flory radius and density_(in/out) can be calculated to be –0.36.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of STORM imaging data and FLIM-FRET measurements.

claim: Molecules with molecular weights greater than 50 kDa (MUC1, CD44, F174B, VCAM1, EPHB1) were similarly excluded at the virus-cell interface to an average approximately 80% reduction.
source: Density_(in/out) was found to be similarly low for groups of membrane proteins, and molecules with molecular weights greater than 50 kDa (MUC1, CD44, F174B, VCAM1, EPHB1, all tagged with SNAP) were similarly excluded at the virus-cell interface to an average ~80% reduction (Figure 6GH).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of STORM imaging data showing protein distribution at virus-cell interfaces.

claim: VAMP2 and LCK10 showed much higher density_(in/out), suggesting that only very low amounts of both of these molecules were excluded.
source: In contrast, much higher density_(in/out) was observed for VAMP2, a SNAP-tagged-only control molecule, and LCK10, a control molecule without any ectodomain, respectively, suggesting that only very low amounts of both of these molecules were excluded.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of STORM imaging data showing protein distribution at virus-cell interfaces.

claim: Various types of glycoproteins have been suggested to inhibit viral infection of cells via steric repulsion.
source: Various types of glycoproteins have been suggested to inhibit viral infection of cells via steric repulsion.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as background knowledge and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: A wide range of glycoproteins individually had a strong inhibitory effect on infection.
source: We found that a wide range of glycoproteins individually had a strong inhibitory effect on infection
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental infection assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The total amount of glycans was negatively correlated with the infection level in each cell.
source: while on the other hand, the total amount of glycans was negatively correlated with the infection level in each cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging and flow cytometry assays.

claim: The infection-inhibitory effect of glycoproteins was molecularly nonspecific but was additively enhanced according to the amount of glycans on the cell surface.
source: Thus, the infection-inhibitory effect of glycoproteins was molecularly nonspecific but was additively enhanced according to the amount of glycans on the cell surface.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of multiple different glycoproteins.

claim: The repulsion between proteins created by branched glycans forms a kinetic energy barrier against packing the virus into the region of protein interstitial space.
source: we conclude that the repulsion between proteins created by branched glycans forms a kinetic energy barrier against packing the virus into the region of protein interstitial space.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations and theoretical modeling.

claim: The formation of the adhesive interface between the virus and the cell membrane, which is necessary for infection, is inhibited by glycans.
source: As a result, the formation of the adhesive interface between the virus and the cell membrane, which is necessary for infection, is inhibited.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of virus binding and infection.

claim: Mucin-related glycoproteins have been suggested as host-side factors in COVID-19 by cellular CRISPR screens and genome-wide association studies.
source: Mucin-related glycoproteins are among the latter group, as suggested by cellular CRISPR screens as well as by genome-wide association studies (Biering et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Biering et al., 2022).

claim: A variety of glycoproteins negatively regulate viral infection in a wide range of systems.
source: These results demonstrate that a variety of glycoproteins negatively regulate viral infection in a wide range of systems.
evidence: The claim is based on synthesis of multiple cited studies on glycoprotein function in viral infection.

claim: Glycoprotein groups that inhibit viral infection have no common amino acid sequences or domains.
source: These glycoprotein groups have no common amino acid sequences or domains.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge from the literature about glycoprotein structures.

claim: The glycans modified by infection-inhibitory proteins include both N-glycans conjugated with asparagine and O-glycans conjugated with serine and threonine.
source: The glycans modified by these proteins include both N-glycans conjugated with asparagine and O-glycans conjugated with serine and threonine.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about glycan chemistry.

claim: Synthetic polymers that bind to cell membranes have been shown to modulate viral infection in a manner dependent on molecular size and molecular density.
source: Indeed, synthetic polymers that bind to cell membranes have been shown to modulate viral infection in a manner dependent on molecular size and molecular density (Kaizuka and Machida, 2023; Pyrć et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Kaizuka and Machida, 2023; Pyrć et al., 2021).

claim: The Forster distance for ATTO 488 and PlasMem Bright Red was estimated to be 6.45 nm in the experimental setting.
source: Then, we went through the above procedure and estimated the effective Ro for ATTO 488 and PlasMem Bright Red to be 6.45 nm.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from FLIM-FRET experimental data.

claim: The Forster distance for ATTO488 and MemGlow 590 was determined as 5.68 nm.
source: Ro for ATTO488 and MemGlow 590 was determined as 5.68 nm, calculated from optical and spectral information of the two dyes (Wu and Brand, 1994).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from optical and spectral data, with citation to the method (Wu and Brand, 1994).

claim: The longest estimated Flory radius that could be resolved by FLIM-FRET was 7.5 nm.
source: The longest estimated RF that could be resolved was 7.5 nm.
evidence: The claim is based on the technical limitations of the FLIM-FRET measurement method.

claim: Molecules with barely detectable FRET changes (e.g. MUC1 [14TR, 42TR], CD44) were expected to be larger than 7.5 nm.
source: Molecules with barely detectable FRET changes (e.g. MUC1 [14TR, 42TR], CD44) were expected to be larger than this maximum measurable distance and were not included in the analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from FLIM-FRET measurement limitations.

claim: The Flory radius of some glycoproteins (e.g. CD43) was smaller than the receptor-ligand binding length of ACE2 and Spike (~27 nm), yet they inhibited viral infection.
source: Importantly, RF of some glycoproteins (e.g. CD43) was found to be smaller than the receptor-ligand binding length of ACE2 and Spike (~27 nm), yet they inhibited viral infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM-FRET measurements and comparison with known protein dimensions.

claim: Glycosylation increases the size of the protein at equilibrium, but the change in Flory radius is slight (e.g., a 1.3-fold increase for one of the longest ectodomains with N=4000).
source: This shift in ν indicates that glycosylation increases the size of the protein at equilibrium, but the change in RF is slight, for example, a 1.3-fold increase for one of the longest ectodomains with N=4000 when these values of ν are applied.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation using the Flory model with experimentally determined scaling exponents.

claim: The measured Flory radii were consistent with or smaller than those calculated from the Alpha Fold predictions.
source: Among the molecules we tested, the measured RF were consistent with or smaller than those calculated from the Alpha Fold predictions (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental FLIM-FRET data with computational predictions.

claim: Molecules such as VCAM1 and EPHB1 had end-to-end distances in predicted conformations much larger than the Flory radius estimated from measurements.
source: However, there were molecules, such as VCAM1 and EPHB1, for which the end-to-end distance in conformation was predicted to be much larger than the Flory radius estimated in our measurements (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental FLIM-FRET data with Alpha Fold 2 predictions.

claim: Low glycosylated proteins such as EPHB1 and VCAM1 tend to consist of multiple folded domains connected by flexible linkers.
source: Many of the molecules in this class are low glycosylated and tend to consist of multiple folded domains connected by flexible linkers, as seen in VCAM1 and EPHB1 (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Alpha Fold 2 predicted structures.

claim: Highly glycosylated proteins such as MUC1 (0TR) were predicted to be more globular and have fewer folded domains.
source: In contrast, the highly glycosylated proteins such as MUC1 (0TR) were predicted to be more globular and have fewer folded domains (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Alpha Fold 2 predicted structures.

claim: Protein glycosylation may reduce the diversity of protein conformational space.
source: This may suggest that protein glycosylation reduces the diversity of protein conformational space.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from differences between measured and predicted protein sizes.

claim: Protein glycosylation may be caused by the intramolecular interactions between amino acids and domain folding being interfered with by the glycans.
source: This may be caused by the intramolecular interactions between amino acids and domain folding being interfered with by the glycans.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for how glycosylation affects protein conformation.

claim: The saturated protein density observed in the in vitro reconstitution experiments is lower than or at most comparable to the actual brush transition density.
source: Based on these, we speculate that the saturated protein density observed in our experiments is lower than or at most comparable to the actual brush transition density.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparison of experimental data with previously reported brush transition densities.

claim: Crowded proteins may be restricted from free random motion but are not significantly extended as in the condensed brush state.
source: Thus, although these crowded proteins may be restricted from free random motion, they are not significantly extended as in the condensed brush state, in which the contribution of resistance to molecular extension fel is expected to be small relative to the overall free energy of the system.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental binding data and comparison with polymer brush theory.

claim: Highly glycosylated molecules (e.g. MUC1) can form brush structures in cells when such proteins are expressed at very high densities.
source: in fact, highly glycosylated molecules (e.g. MUC1) can form brush structures in cells when such proteins are expressed at very high densities (Shurer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Shurer et al., 2019).

claim: Cells containing brushed glycoproteins transformed the cell membrane into a shape with an enormous amount of tubular structure.
source: In addition, cells containing brushed glycoproteins also transformed the cell membrane into a shape with an enormous amount of tubular structure.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge from cited literature about cells with high glycoprotein expression.

claim: Membrane tubules generated upon the insertion of polymers in membranes were neither inhibitory nor activating on viral infection.
source: We also note that it has been previously shown that membrane tubules generated upon the insertion of polymers in membranes were neither inhibitory nor activating on viral infection (Kaizuka and Machida, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Kaizuka and Machida, 2023).

claim: Membrane tubules generated by overcrowded glycocalyx are on the ~μm scale, much larger than viruses.
source: This is simply because these tubular structures are on the ~μm scale, and much larger than viruses, and we assumed that this logic can also be applied to membrane tubules generated by overcrowded glycocalyx (Shurer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited literature and comparison of size scales.

claim: Molecules may become locally and instantaneously crowded in the vicinity of the virus-cell interface during molecular exclusion.
source: As a result, we speculate that molecules may become locally and instantaneously crowded in the vicinity of the interface.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for how molecular exclusion creates local crowding.

claim: If the density increase is sufficiently large, glycosylated molecules may experience strong intermolecular repulsion, preventing them from being packed together with the virus.
source: If the density increase is sufficiently large, the glycosylated molecules may experience strong intermolecular repulsion, preventing them from being packed together with the virus.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for how glycosylation inhibits interface formation.

claim: Molecules with low glycosylation may be readily distorted and accept crowding by being brushed.
source: On the other hand, molecules with low glycosylation may be readily distorted and accept crowding by being brushed.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for how low glycosylation allows interface formation.

claim: The energy barrier U* required for the virus to form an interface with the cell is increased by glycosylation of membrane proteins in the plasma membrane, thereby suppressing infection.
source: We hypothesize that the energy barrier U* required for the virus to form an interface with the cell is increased by glycosylation of membrane proteins in the plasma membrane, thereby suppressing infection.
evidence: The claim is the main hypothesis of the study, based on synthesis of multiple experimental observations and theoretical considerations.

claim: The driving force for molecular exclusion from the virus-cell interface may be the adhesion energy of the interfacial membrane.
source: The driving force for this molecular exclusion may be the adhesion energy of the interfacial membrane.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a physical mechanism for molecular exclusion.

claim: There are many viruses that bind to cells but are not taken up due to insufficient molecular exclusion at the interface.
source: In reality, however, there are many viruses that bind to cells but are not taken up due to insufficient molecular exclusion at the interface (Figure 3A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of virus binding and infection.

claim: A possible factor creating an energy barrier to molecular exclusion is the strong viscosity of the plasma membrane, experimentally confirmed to be on the scale of ~1 µm2/s.
source: A possible factor creating an energy barrier to molecular exclusion is the strong viscosity of the plasma membrane, experimentally confirmed to be on the scale of ~1 µm2/s (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of protein diffusion on membranes.

claim: When molecular exclusion from the interface bond center to the periphery proceeds, viscous stress is generated to resist the movement.
source: In such an environment of strong viscosity, when molecular exclusion from the interface bond center to the periphery proceeds, viscous stress is generated to resist the movement (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from membrane viscosity measurements and physical principles.

claim: Viscous stress is created in the lipid bilayer and is common to all transmembrane molecules, regardless of protein glycosylation.
source: Viscous stress, however, is created in the lipid bilayer and is common to all transmembrane molecules, regardless of protein glycosylation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from physical principles about membrane viscosity.
